subject: polity
title: Landmark Supreme Court Judgments
description: 7 Landmark Cases Every UPSC Aspirant Should Know — Kesavananda Bharati, Maneka Gandhi, Minerva Mills, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, I.R. Coelho, Puttaswamy

content.overview: Landmark Supreme Court judgments that shaped Indian constitutional law. Each case below covers Background, Key Issues, Judgment, Key Principles, and Significance.
keyPoints: KESAVANANDA BHARATI CASE (1973) — Theme: Constitutional Amendments & Basic Structure Doctrine
Kesavananda Background: Kerala government acquired land belonging to Edneer Mutt (managed by Kesavananda Bharati); larger question — how far can Parliament amend the Constitution?
Kesavananda Key Issues: Does Parliament have unlimited power to amend? Can Fundamental Rights be amended or taken away?
Kesavananda Judgment: Parliament can amend under Article 368, but cannot destroy or alter the Basic Structure; both FRs and DPSPs can be amended, but Basic Structure must be preserved

Basic Structure includes (illustrative): Supremacy of the Constitution, Republican & democratic form of government, Secularism, Separation of powers, Judicial review, Federalism, Unity and integrity of India
Kesavananda Significance: Introduced Basic Structure Doctrine; placed limits on Parliament's amending power — 'Constitution can be amended, but not destroyed'
MANEKA GANDHI CASE (1978) — Theme: Fundamental Rights (Article 21)
Maneka Background: Passport impounded by government under Passports Act 1967; she challenged it under Articles 21, 14 and 19
Maneka Key Issues: Does 'procedure established by law' mean ANY procedure, or must it be fair, just and reasonable? Can personal liberty be restricted without a just procedure?
Maneka Judgment: Procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable, not arbitrary; linked Article 21 with Articles 14 and 19; expanded 'personal liberty' to include right to travel abroad
Maneka Key Principles: Article 21 has wider meaning; Articles 14, 19 and 21 are interlinked — the 'Golden Triangle'; personal liberty includes rights that make life meaningful
Maneka Significance: Strengthened FR protection; State cannot deprive liberty arbitrarily — 'Procedure must be fair, just and reasonable for true freedom'
MINERVA MILLS CASE (1980) — Theme: Amendment Power & Balance between FRs and DPSPs
Minerva Background: Challenge to 42nd Amendment Act 1976, which gave Parliament unlimited amending power and placed DPSPs over FRs; challenged by Minerva Mills textile company
Minerva Judgment: Struck down key provisions of 42nd Amendment; Parliament's amending power is limited and cannot destroy Basic Structure; FRs and DPSPs are complementary and must be kept in balance
Minerva Key Principles: FRs and DPSPs are complementary, not antagonistic; established principle of balance between individual rights and social goals
Minerva Significance: Reaffirmed Basic Structure Doctrine; prevented Parliament from acquiring unlimited amending power — 'Rights and principles must go hand in hand for a just society'
S.R. BOMMAI CASE (1994) — Theme: Federalism

Bommai Background: S.R. Bommai was CM of Karnataka; Union dismissed his government under Article 356 alleging breakdown of constitutional machinery; petitions challenged misuse of Article 356 by the Centre
Bommai Key Issues: Can the President impose President's Rule on subjective satisfaction? Is the proclamation justiciable? What are the limits on Centre's power to dismiss a State government?

Bommai Judgment: President's satisfaction under Article 356 is subject to judicial review; Centre cannot dismiss a State government arbitrarily or for political reasons; federalism is part of the Basic Structure; floor test in Legislative Assembly is the proper way to test majority
Bommai Key Principles: Article 356 is an extraordinary power, not a routine political tool; Court can restore a dismissed government if proclamation is found unconstitutional
Bommai Significance: Put an end to arbitrary use of Article 356; strengthened federal structure — 'Federalism is the foundation of India's unity in diversity'
VISHAKA CASE (1997) — Theme: Protection against Sexual Harassment at Workplace
Vishaka Background: PIL filed by Vishaka and other women's groups after the brutal gang rape of a social worker in Rajasthan; no specific laws at that time to address workplace sexual harassment

Vishaka Key Issues: Does sexual harassment at the workplace violate Fundamental Rights? Can international conventions fill the gap in domestic law? What guidelines can be issued in absence of specific legislation?

Vishaka Judgment: SC laid down Vishaka Guidelines; sexual harassment violates Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21; directed employers to create safe working environment and set up Complaints Committees in every workplace

Vishaka Key Principles: Right to a safe and dignified working environment is a Fundamental Right; harassment includes unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of sexual nature; employers must take preventive steps; Guidelines binding until Parliament enacts a law
Vishaka Significance: Influenced the enactment of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 — 'A safe workplace is a right, not a privilege'
I.R. COELHO CASE (2007): Laws placed in the 9th Schedule after 24 April 1973 are subject to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure
PUTTASWAMY CASE (2017): Right to Privacy is a Fundamental Right under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution

mnemonics.trick: K-M-M-B-V-C-P = Kesavananda (1973), Maneka (1978), Minerva (1980), Bommai (1994), Vishaka (1997), Coelho (2007), Puttaswamy (2017)
mnemonics.explanation: Chronological order of the 7 landmark cases: 1973 Kesavananda, 1978 Maneka, 1980 Minerva, 1994 Bommai, 1997 Vishaka, 2007 Coelho, 2017 Puttaswamy

mnemonics.trick: S-R-S-S-J-F-U = Supremacy, Republican-democratic, Secularism, Separation of powers, Judicial review, Federalism, Unity & integrity
mnemonics.explanation: Basic Structure includes: Supremacy of Constitution, Republican & democratic government, Secularism, Separation of powers, Judicial review, Federalism, Unity and integrity of India
Articles 14, 19 and 21 are interlinked and form the 'Golden Triangle' — Maneka Gandhi case

mnemonics.trick: 14-15-19(1)(g)-21 = Equality, No discrimination, Practice profession, Life with dignity
mnemonics.explanation: Sexual harassment at workplace violates Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 — Vishaka case

quiz.question: Which case established the 'Basic Structure' doctrine?
quiz.explanation: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) established the basic structure doctrine

quiz.question: The 'Golden Triangle' of Articles 14, 19 and 21 was established in:
quiz.explanation: Maneka Gandhi case (1978) established that Articles 14, 19 and 21 are interlinked — the 'Golden Triangle'

quiz.question: Which case dealt with the challenge to the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
quiz.explanation: Minerva Mills case (1980) struck down key provisions of the 42nd Amendment

quiz.question: In S.R. Bommai case, the Court held that majority of a government must be tested:
options: On the floor of the Assembly
quiz.explanation: S.R. Bommai case (1994) held that the floor test in the Legislative Assembly is the proper way to test majority

quiz.question: Vishaka Guidelines were replaced by which Act in 2013?
quiz.explanation: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) followed the Vishaka Guidelines

quiz.question: Right to privacy was declared a Fundamental Right in which case?
quiz.explanation: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) declared right to privacy a Fundamental Right under Article 21

quiz.question: Which case held that 9th Schedule laws are subject to judicial review?
quiz.explanation: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that laws in the 9th Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure

timeline.event: Kesavananda Bharati case - Basic Structure doctrine
S.R. Bommai case - Article 356 judicial review
